inline_comments.comment: The comment only explains half the condition. It says "Early return if the code is already transformed" but the actual guard is `isAlreadyTransformed && !hasNamedExports`—meaning the early return is skipped when there are still named exports that need to be merged into the factory call. The `!hasNamedExports` part is non-obvious; a reader could reasonably expect the function to bail out whenever it detects the factory call is already in place. Adding a second sentence to the comment would clarify: e.g., "Skip only when there are no named exports left to fold into the factory call; if named exports remain, fall through to let the merge scenarios handle them."

general_comments.comment: The early return is placed before the import-fixup block, so any file that is structurally transformed (has the `defineMain`/`definePreview` call) but has a missing or incomplete import will be silently returned unchanged. Two test cases in the test file directly verify the expected behavior for these scenarios: `'should add missing import when already transformed but import is absent'` and `'should add missing specifier when already transformed but defineMain is not in existing import'`. Both tests would fail with this diff applied. The fix should either (a) also require a valid import before returning early, or (b) restructure the function so that the import-fixup pass always runs independently of whether the structural transformation is skipped.

The condition `isAlreadyTransformed && !hasNamedExports` treats `main` and `preview` config types identically. The intended design (visible in the more complete version of this logic) differentiates them: for `main` configs, the transform is always skipped when already transformed (even with lingering named exports), whereas for `preview` configs the skip is conditional on there being no named exports to merge. As written, a `main` config that is already wrapped but still has a stray named export (e.g., `export const tags = []` alongside `export default defineMain({})`) would be re-processed unnecessarily. This is functionally safe but inconsistent with the stated design intent and warrants a comment or an explicit `configType` branch.
